THOUGHT: This 36-year-old woman presents with a painless, progressively enlarging neck mass for 3 months, located on the left side of the neck and moving with swallowing — a classic sign of thyroid origin. The absence of systemic B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), no history of radiation, no hoarseness or dysphagia, and normal vital signs argue against aggressive infection, lymphoma, or advanced malignancy. Physical exam reveals a firm, irregular, non-tender 2.5-cm mass; irregularity and firmness raise concern for malignancy, though not diagnostic alone. Neck ultrasound shows a solitary left lobe thyroid nodule with two suspicious features: increased vascularity and hyperechoic punctate regions (i.e., microcalcifications) — both are well-established sonographic red flags for papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). While FNA biopsy is pending (and remains the diagnostic gold standard), clinical and imaging findings strongly converge on a malignant thyroid nodule. Among thyroid malignancies, papillary thyroid carcinoma is by far the most common (~80–85% of cases), especially in young to middle-aged women, and is classically associated with microcalcifications and increased vascularity on ultrasound. Follicular thyroid carcinoma typically lacks microcalcifications and is less likely to present with such clear sonographic malignancy features; medullary and anaplastic carcinomas are far less common and usually present with more aggressive features (e.g., family history, rapid growth, hoarseness, or systemic symptoms) — none of which are present here.

DIAGNOSIS: Papillary thyroid carcinoma
